'''Delmer Lawrence Daves''' (July 24, 1904 – August 17, 1977) was an American [[screenwriter]], [[film director]] and [[film producer]].<ref name="EB">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Delmer-Daves |title=Delmer Daves |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |location=Edinburgh |access-date=10 May 2021}}</ref> He worked in many [[Film genre|genres]], including [[film noir]] and [[war film|warfare]], but he is best known for his [[Western (genre)|Western movies]], especially ''[[Broken Arrow (1950 film)|Broken Arrow]]'' (1950), ''[[The Last Wagon (1956 film)|The Last Wagon]]'' (1956), ''[[3:10 to Yuma (1957 film)|3:10 to Yuma]]'' (1957) and ''[[The Hanging Tree (film)|The Hanging Tree]]'' (1959). He was required to work exclusively on studio-based films after heart trouble in 1959, one of which, ''[[A Summer Place (film)|A Summer Place]]'' (1959), was a huge commercial success.

Daves worked with some of the best known players of his time including established stars like [[Humphrey Bogart]], [[Gary Cooper]], [[Glenn Ford]], [[James Stewart]] and [[Richard Widmark]]. He also helped to develop the careers of up-and-coming players such as [[Ernest Borgnine]], [[Charles Bronson]], [[Felicia Farr]] and [[George C. Scott]].

==Life and career==
===College and acting===
Born in [[San Francisco]], Daves graduated from [[Stanford University]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=1977-08-19 |title=SERVICES TOMORROW FOR DELMER L DAVES (Published 1977) |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1977/08/19/archives/services-tomorrow-for-delmer-l-daves-motion-picture-producer-writer.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230829053505/https://www.nytimes.com/1977/08/19/archives/services-tomorrow-for-delmer-l-daves-motion-picture-producer-writer.html |archive-date=August 29, 2023 |access-date=2024-03-06 |language=en}}</ref> His first job in the film industry was [[Prop (stage, screen)|prop boy]] on the [[Western (genre)|Western]] ''[[The Covered Wagon]]'' (1923), directed by [[James Cruze]], and then served as a [[technical advisor]] on a number of other films.<ref name="RDM">{{cite news |last=McCann |first=Richard Dyer |title=Delmer Daves Recalls His Route to the Top: Hollywood Letter |work=The Christian Science Monitor |date=March 11, 1958 |page=11}}</ref> He tried his hand at acting and appeared in more than ten movies including ''[[The Night Flyer (film)|The Night Flyer]]'' (1928) (produced by Cruze), ''[[The Duke Steps Out]]'' (1929) and ''[[Good News (1930 film)|Good News]]'' (1930).<ref name="EB"/><ref name="RDM"/>

===Screenwriting===
While he was acting, Daves was given the opportunity by [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer|MGM]] to collaborate on [[screenplay]]s. He began his career as a screenwriter by contributing to the early sound comedy film ''[[So This Is College]]'' (MGM; 1929), directed by [[Sam Wood]]. Later, working for MGM and other companies, he wrote screenplays for films like ''[[Shipmates (film)|Shipmates]]'' (MGM; 1931), ''[[Dames (film)|Dames]]'' ([[Warner Bros]]; 1934), ''[[The Petrified Forest]]'' (Warner Bros; 1936), ''[[Love Affair (1939 film)|Love Affair]]'' ([[RKO Radio Pictures|RKO Radio]]; 1939), and ''[[You Were Never Lovelier]]'' ([[Columbia Pictures|Columbia]]; 1942).<ref name="EB"/><ref name="RDM"/> Daves was particularly successful with ''Love Affair'' which, using his original script, was remade as ''[[An Affair to Remember]]'' ([[20th Century Fox]]; 1957).<ref>{{cite book |last=Vermilye |first=Jerry |title=Cary Grant |publisher=Galahad Books |location=New York City |year=1973 |page=123 |isbn=978-08-83652-91-6}}</ref>

===Direction===
In 1943, Warner Bros asked Daves to direct ''[[Destination Tokyo]]'', a [[war film|wartime adventure]] film starring [[Cary Grant]] and [[John Garfield]]. Daves assisted with the screenplay and this became normal practice for him as a director.<ref name="EB"/><ref name="BT">{{cite journal |last=Tavernier |first=Bertrand |title=The ethical romantic |journal=Film Comment |location=New York City |date=January 2003 |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=42–49 |url=https://www.filmcomment.com/article/delmer-daves-bertrand-tavernier/}}</ref> He directed three more films during the [[World War II|Second World War]] – ''[[The Very Thought of You (film)|The Very Thought of You]]'' (1944), ''[[Hollywood Canteen (film)|Hollywood Canteen]]'' (1944) and ''[[Pride of the Marines (film)|Pride of the Marines]]'' (1945), all for Warners. The first two of those were light-hearted but the latter, starring John Garfield and [[Eleanor Parker]], studied the difficulties faced by a [[US marine]] who had been blinded at the [[Battle of Guadalcanal]].<ref name="EB"/> All four of Daves' wartime films were commercially successful.<ref>{{cite news |last=Lusk |first=Norbert |title=Daves Clicks as Director |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |date=January 11, 1944 |page=8}}</ref> After the war, Daves turned to [[film noir]] and made ''[[The Red House (film)|The Red House]]'' (1947), starring [[Edward G. Robinson]], for [[Sol Lesser]] at [[United Artists]].<ref name="EB"/> He returned to Warners where he wrote and directed ''[[Dark Passage (film)|Dark Passage]]'' (1947), starring [[Humphrey Bogart]], [[Lauren Bacall]] and [[Agnes Moorehead]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=2016-05-27 |title=1940s Dispatches From the Land of Wynken, Blynken and Noir (Published 2016) |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/29/movies/1940s-dispatches-from-the-land-of-wynken-blynken-and-noir.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221018090402/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/29/movies/1940s-dispatches-from-the-land-of-wynken-blynken-and-noir.html |archive-date=October 18, 2022 |access-date=2024-03-06 |language=en |last1=Hoberman |first1=J. }}</ref> He later directed ''[[To the Victor]]'' (1948), ''[[A Kiss in the Dark (1949 film)|A Kiss in the Dark]]'' (1949) and ''[[Task Force (film)|Task Force]]'' (1949). He also wrote the screenplay for ''Task Force'', which starred [[Gary Cooper]].<ref name="EB"/>

In February 1949, Daves signed a long-term contract at [[20th Century Fox]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Vera Ralston to Join John Wayne in 'Eagles;' 20th Signs Delmer Daves |author=Schallert, Edwin |date=February 24, 1949 |work=Los Angeles Times |page=21}}</ref> He began by directing his first [[Western (genre)|Western]], the critically acclaimed ''[[Broken Arrow (1950 film)|Broken Arrow]]'' (1950) which starred [[James Stewart]], [[Debra Paget]] and [[Jeff Chandler]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Steigers Act Out Breakup of a Marriage: Breakup Acted Out by Steigers |author=Loynd, Ray |work=Los Angeles Times |date=June 27, 1969 |page=d1}}</ref> Chandler played [[Cochise]] and the movie's success inspired the making of other films with [[Native Americans in the United States|Native American]] protagonists.<ref name="EB"/> [[Kim Newman]] wrote that, by his dignified and heroic performance, Oscar-nominated Chandler established Cochise as "the 1950s model of an Indian hero".{{sfn|Newman|1990|p=70}} Newman points out that the film inspired goodwill to other Native American chiefs such as [[Sitting Bull]], [[Crazy Horse]] and [[Geronimo]] – as a result, "it became fashionable for Westerns to be pro-Indian". {{sfn|Newman|1990|p=71}} Other scholars warned that these "pro-Indian" movies proposed that peaceful co-existence between Natives and whites was achieved only through the loss of Indian identity. "Good" Indians would conform to white society, "bad" Indians would not.<ref name="Aleiss">{{cite book |last=Aleiss |first=Angela |title=Making the White Man's Indian: Native Americans and Hollywood Movies |publisher=Praeger Publishers |date=2005 |pages=90–96 |isbn=978-02-75983-96-3 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=m1-JDrrM6mIC&dq=an+indian+love+story+1911&pg=PA11}}</ref>

Daves decided to try other genres with the adventure films ''[[Bird of Paradise (1951 film)|Bird of Paradise]]'' (1951) and ''[[Treasure of the Golden Condor]]'' (1953), both of which he wrote and directed.<ref name="EB"/> As director only, he made ''[[Never Let Me Go (1953 film)|Never Let Me Go]]'' (1953) for MGM and ''[[Demetrius and the Gladiators]]'' (1954) for Fox.<ref name="EB"/> ''Never Let Me Go'', starring [[Clark Gable]] and [[Gene Tierney]], was shot entirely in England and featured a supporting cast of well-known British actors.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/title/3495/never-let-me-go |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120318202913/http://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/title/3495/Never-Let-Me-Go/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=March 18, 2012 |title=Never Let Me Go |publisher=Turner Classic Movies |access-date=12 July 2021}}</ref>

Daves became a freelance director in 1954 and returned to Warners to work on ''[[Drum Beat (film)|Drum Beat]]'' (1954), which he wrote, directed and also co-produced with [[Alan Ladd]], who starred in the movie. One of Ladd's co-stars was [[Charles Bronson]] who, then relatively unknown, gave an impressive performance as the [[Modoc people|Modoc]] chief [[Kintpuash|Captain Jack]].<ref name="EB"/><ref>{{cite news |last=Scheuer |first=Philip K. |title='Drum Beat' Superior Frontier Melodrama |work=Los Angeles Times |date=November 11, 1954 |page=A13}}</ref> By this time, Daves was fed up of the "pro-Indian" fashion that he had begun, and ''Drum Beat'' was "pro-settler" with the hanging of Bronson's character in the final scene "restoring the balance".{{sfn|Newman|1990|p=72}} Aleiss argued that ''Drum Beat'' actually preached the same theme in his previous Westerns of good Indians conforming to white expectations while eliminating the bad Indian (Captain Jack).<ref name="Aleiss"/> Daves worked primarily on Westerns for the next five years.<ref name="BT"/>

After writing the screenplay of ''[[White Feather (film)|White Feather]]'' (1955) for Fox, Daves directed three highly rated Westerns: ''[[Jubal (film)|Jubal]]'' (1956) for Columbia; ''[[The Last Wagon (1956 film)|The Last Wagon]]'' (1956) for Fox; and ''[[3:10 to Yuma (1957 film)|3:10 to Yuma]]'' (1957) for Columbia. He co-wrote the screenplay for the first two of these; Halsted Welles adapted ''3:10 to Yuma'' from the novel by [[Elmore Leonard]]. [[Felicia Farr]] had a significant role in all three films. [[Glenn Ford]] was the lead actor in ''Jubal'' and co-starred with [[Van Heflin]] in ''3:10 to Yuma''. [[Richard Widmark]] starred in ''The Last Wagon''. [[Ernest Borgnine]], Charles Bronson and [[Rod Steiger]] were all in ''Jubal''; [[James Drury]] had a small part in ''The Last Wagon''; [[Richard Jaeckel]] and [[Leora Dana]] had significant parts in ''3:10 to Yuma''. According to one review, ''3:10 to Yuma'' was a variation on ''[[High Noon]]'' (1952) as it "pits a farmer (Heflin) in a battle of wits with a captured killer" (Ford, cast against type as a villain) – it is a "psychological Western" that is generally considered a classic of the genre.<ref name="EB"/>

Following ''[[Cowboy (1958 film)|Cowboy]]'' (1958) which again starred Glenn Ford, this time with Felicia Farr's future husband [[Jack Lemmon]], Daves decided on a switch of genre to direct ''[[Kings Go Forth]]'' (1958) a World War II drama for United Artists which starred [[Frank Sinatra]], [[Tony Curtis]] and [[Natalie Wood]]. Daves returned to Westerns towards the end of 1958 when he made ''[[The Badlanders]]'' (1958) for MGM. This film was in effect a remake of noir classic ''[[The Asphalt Jungle]]'' (1950), reset in the 1890s. It starred Alan Ladd and Ernest Borgnine.<ref name="EB"/>

Daves then made his last Western, ''[[The Hanging Tree (film)|The Hanging Tree]]'' (1959) starring Gary Cooper, [[Maria Schell]] and [[Karl Malden]], with [[George C. Scott]] making his debut. This is regarded as another classic and Daves made full use of a stark landscape in which the only real feature was a makeshift gold camp.{{sfn|Newman|1990|p=18}} The power of newly struck gold sends the community into a frenzy and they become, in Newman's words, "a wild collection of riotous scum".{{sfn|Newman|1990|p=18}}

Daves suffered problems with his heart<ref name="DK"/> during the making of ''The Hanging Tree'' and was forced to step aside for several days; Malden took over as director while Daves was absent. There has been speculation that health problems prevented Daves from continuing to work on Westerns, which were often physically demanding.<ref name="EB"/>

===Later films===
On medical advice, Daves decided to forgo Westerns and limit himself to studio-bound productions which were less strenuous.<ref name="DK">{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/01/27/movies/homevideo/27dvds.html |last=Kehr |first=Dave |title=Critic's Choice – New DVDs: Romance Classics |work=New York Times |date=26 January 2009 |access-date=12 May 2021}}</ref> He wrote, produced and directed a series of romantic dramas at Warners which all starred [[Troy Donahue]]: ''[[A Summer Place (film)|A Summer Place]]'' (1959), ''[[Parrish (film)|Parrish]]'' (1961),  ''[[Susan Slade]]'' (1961) and ''[[Rome Adventure]]'' (1962).<ref name="DK"/> ''A Summer Place'' was one of his biggest commercial successes. Based on the novel by [[Sloan Wilson]], it was controversial at the time for its treatment of adultery and pre-marital sex.<ref name="EB"/><ref name="DK"/>

Daves' final three films were all made at Warners. ''[[Spencer's Mountain]]'' (1963) starred [[Henry Fonda]] and [[Maureen O'Hara]]. It was based upon [[Earl Hamner Jr.|Earl Hamner Jr's]] autobiographical novel of the same name, and served as the basis for the later television series ''[[The Waltons]]''.<ref>{{cite news |last=Schumach |first=Murray |title=Hollywood's Literary Set |newspaper=New York Times |date=May 19, 1963 |page=X7}}</ref> Daves then wrote, directed and produced ''[[Youngblood Hawke (film)|Youngblood Hawke]]'' (1964) and ''[[The Battle of the Villa Fiorita]]'' (1965). He retired after ''Villa Fiorita'' was released.<ref name="DK"/>

Daves was married to actress [[Mary Lawrence (actor)|Mary Lawrence]] from 1938 until he died on August 17, 1977. He is interred at the [[Forest Lawn Memorial Park (Glendale)|Forest Lawn Memorial Park Cemetery]] in [[Glendale, California]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Delmer Daves, Motion Picture Executive, Actor |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=August 19, 1977 |page=C8}}</ref>

==Legacy==
[[Kim Newman]] says of Daves and [[Anthony Mann]] that they were able to "ring changes" on seemingly familiar Western storylines by "playing up the psychologically acute reflections of their characters" in relation to the landscape as well as to each other. Daves, he says, achieved this in each of ''Broken Arrow'', ''The Last Wagon'', ''3:10 to Yuma'', and ''The Hanging Tree''.{{sfn|Newman|1990|p=xvi}}

Despite several highly acclaimed films, [[Dave Kehr]] considers Daves to be an under-rated and neglected filmmaker.<ref name="DK"/> As a director, Daves first built his reputation on morally complex war films such as ''Pride of the Marines'' and socially progressive Westerns. For example, ''Broken Arrow'' has been credited as one of the first to introduce the issue of racism in post-war American movies, and it is widely regarded as one of the first "pro-Native American" films.<ref name="DK"/> Kehr views Daves' late period romances as sharing the same virtues as his earlier action films: "characters composed with the utmost integrity and respect; a gift for creating a detailed and convincing social background; and a strong, clear narrative style that allowed him to manage a large cast of characters and several simultaneous levels of dramatic events".<ref name="DK"/>
